Selecting and interpreting a shallow neural network

Source: vignettes/selection-workflow.Rmd
selection-workflow.Rmd

The usual statnnet workflow selects a parsimonious network before constructing regression-style summaries. The example uses the bundled Auto MPG data and a small search so that the vignette can be rebuilt quickly.

library(nnet)
library(statnnet)

data("auto_mpg", package = "statnnet")

analysis_data <- auto_mpg
continuous_variables <- c(
  "mpg", "displacement", "horsepower", "weight", "acceleration",
  "model_year"
)
analysis_data[continuous_variables] <- scale(
  analysis_data[continuous_variables]
)

Select inputs and hidden-layer size

select_nnet() alternates between hidden-layer and input selection using an information criterion. Formula terms are selected as groups, so the indicator columns for a factor enter or leave together. Multiple starting values are used for every candidate model; only converged starts are eligible for selection.

selection <- select_nnet(
  mpg ~ cylinders + displacement + horsepower + weight + acceleration +
    model_year + origin,
  data = analysis_data,
  max_size = 5,
  n_starts = 5,
  criterion = "BIC",
  maxit = 1000,
  seed = 2026,
  progress = FALSE
)

selection
#> statnnet model selection
#> Call:
#> select_nnet(x = mpg ~ cylinders + displacement + horsepower + 
#>     weight + acceleration + model_year + origin, data = analysis_data, 
#>     max_size = 5, n_starts = 5, criterion = "BIC", maxit = 1000, 
#>     seed = 2026, progress = FALSE)
#> Selected model: 6 input columns, 2 hidden units, 17 network weights
#> BIC: 316.842; 39 candidate models; 194 converged starts
#> Selected terms: displacement, horsepower, weight, model_year, origin
#> Excluded terms: cylinders, acceleration
summary(selection)
#> statnnet model-selection summary
#> Selected formula: mpg ~ displacement + horsepower + weight + model_year + origin

Check the numerical diagnostics

Converting the result with statnnet() checks the selected nnet fit and reports whether covariance-based summaries are numerically available. Selection is unpenalised, and a converged fit may still have poorly conditioned curvature.

Numerical availability does not show that Wald p-values or delta-method intervals have their nominal coverage. The Gaussian simulations motivating the method favour parsimonious networks, including a hidden layer no larger than the fitted input layer. statnnet() records this comparison and warns when there are more hidden nodes than input nodes. The inferential quantities remain approximate and conditional on the setting studied.

The package can calculate the same summaries for supported binary-response fits, but the package authors have not established their frequentist calibration; binary Wald tests and intervals should therefore be treated as exploratory.

selected_model <- suppressWarnings(statnnet(selection))
selected_model
#> statnnet: statistical summary of a fitted nnet model
#> Formula: mpg ~ displacement + horsepower + weight + model_year + origin
#> Architecture: 6-2-1; 17 weights; n = 392
#> Response: continuous; decay: 0
#> Selection: BIC = 316.842; uncertainty is conditional on the selected model
#> nnet convergence code: 0
#> Covariance: unavailable - the penalised information matrix is not positive definite

Here we refit the selected architecture with a small, pre-specified decay to demonstrate the inferential interface. This decay value is not selected by BIC. In an analysis it should be justified and examined in a sensitivity analysis, while the resulting uncertainty remains conditional on the selected structure, penalty, and local optimum.

regularised_fit <- nnet(
  selection$formula,
  data = analysis_data,
  size = selection$size,
  linout = TRUE,
  decay = 0.02,
  Hess = TRUE,
  Wts = selection$fit$wts,
  maxit = 1000,
  trace = FALSE
)

model <- statnnet(
  regularised_fit,
  data = analysis_data,
  response = "continuous"
)

model
#> statnnet: statistical summary of a fitted nnet model
#> Formula: mpg ~ displacement + horsepower + weight + model_year + origin
#> Architecture: 6-2-1; 17 weights; n = 392
#> Response: continuous; decay: 0.02
#> nnet convergence code: 0
#> Covariance: available (reciprocal condition number 4.65e-05)
summary(model, effects = "none")

Describe the fitted response surface

pce() calculates finite differences of the partial-dependence function. These are descriptive summaries of the fitted network rather than causal effects, and their pointwise intervals are conditional on the modelling choices above.

pce(model, "weight", length_out = 5)
#>   variable contrast       value step   estimate  std_error   conf_low
#> 1   weight     <NA> -1.60652233    1 -0.7382568 0.07535996 -0.8859596
#> 2   weight     <NA> -0.81843976    1 -0.7472244 0.14478001 -1.0309880
#> 3   weight     <NA> -0.03035718    1 -0.4880063 0.06942109 -0.6240691
#> 4   weight     <NA>  0.75772540    1 -0.2402029 0.12157500 -0.4784855
#> 5   weight     <NA>  1.54580798    1 -0.1163020 0.11270499 -0.3371997
#>      conf_high
#> 1 -0.590553970
#> 2 -0.463460833
#> 3 -0.351943430
#> 4 -0.001920282
#> 5  0.104595706
plot(model, "weight", length_out = 25)

The selected model retains the original nnet fit, so ordinary predictions remain available through predict().

head(predict(model, newdata = analysis_data))
#>        [,1]
#> 1 -1.058587
#> 2 -1.196590
#> 3 -1.107343
#> 4 -1.114626
#> 5 -1.083773
#> 6 -1.280884

Citation

Run citation("statnnet") for formatted references and BibTeX entries. If you use select_nnet() for input or hidden-layer selection, cite McInerney and Burke (2025). If you use covariance estimates, Wald summaries, grouped tests, or covariate-effect methods, cite McInerney and Burke (2026). Analyses using both parts of the package should cite both papers.
